Our releases happen in two steps. First we upload every new asset (JS bundles, CSS, images) under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`, alongside the existing files. Then we update the manifest so it points to those new names. The manifest is the only file whose contents change in place. Every asset file is written once and never modified.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch takes effect the moment it lands. Any browser that fetches the new manifest will immediately request whatever files it names. If those files aren't already uploaded, those requests return 404s and users get a broken page. Uploading everything first means the manifest only ever references files that already exist. That makes the switch a single atomic step: users see either the old release or the new one, never a mix.

**Why we keep the old assets:** some browsers loaded the previous manifest before the switch, and they will keep requesting the files it names. This includes open tabs that lazy-load a chunk later, pages served from cache, and CDN edges still holding the old manifest. If we deleted the old files during the release, those sessions would start failing partway through. Leaving them in place lets those users finish on the old version and pick up the new one on their next load. Keeping them also makes rollback trivial: point the manifest back at the previous names and nothing needs to be re-uploaded.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. Because a name never refers to different content, new and old files can sit side by side without overwriting each other, and each file can be cached aggressively.

Our static-site release has two steps, always in this order:

1. **Upload every new asset under a versioned name.** Each file gets a name that changes when its content changes, such as `app.3f9c2a.js` instead of `app.js`. Nothing points to these files yet, so uploading them changes nothing users can see.
2. **Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest tells browsers which asset files make up the current site. Updating it is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload comes before the switch:** once the manifest changes, any browser that loads it will immediately request the files it lists. If those files aren't uploaded yet, the browser gets 404s and the page breaks. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists the moment anyone can see it. The switch then becomes a single small change: users get either the complete old version or the complete new one, never a mix.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the files that manifest lists. This happens with an open tab that lazy-loads a script, with a page served from cache, or with a CDN edge still serving the old manifest. If we deleted those files during the release, those users would break even though they did nothing wrong. Because every version has its own file names, old and new assets can sit side by side without conflict. Keeping the old ones lets in-flight sessions finish on the version they started with.

The versioned names are what make both rules work. New files can't overwrite old ones, so uploading early is safe and keeping old files costs nothing but storage.
